implementation_notes: Ruby's core gives threads and queues, not a composite: map the parts to Thread.new { route(p) } (or push them into a Thread::Queue drained by a fixed worker pool) and then call Thread#value on each thread - it joins the thread and returns the block's value, so the collected array is the aggregation input and a plain inject performs the merge. The GVL means CPU-bound parts do not run truly in parallel, so threads pay off for I/O-bound parts; reach for concurrent-ruby (next variant) when a promise/executor abstraction is wanted instead of raw threads.
pitfalls: Thread#value re-raises the part's exception at the join point while the remaining threads keep running; abort_on_exception only changes visibility, not the semantics.
The GVL serialises CPU-bound work: use threads for I/O-bound parts and processes (or a worker fleet) for CPU-bound ones.
Thread.new per part is unbounded and expensive; a Thread::Queue with N workers is the pool equivalent of the same fan-out.

variants.name: concurrent-ruby Promises zip_futures_over
variants.implementation_notes: concurrent-ruby's Promises expose zip_futures_over(enumerable) { |element| ... }, which becomes resolved after all per-element futures resolve - split, fan-out and barrier in one call; .value! blocks and returns the results array (or re-raises), and the merge is a reduce over it. The library advertises a lock-free synchronization layer, executors with a controllable concurrency level and back-pressure-aware channels, which is what you would otherwise hand-roll on Thread + Queue.
pitfalls: value!/value blocks the calling thread; calling it from inside a promise executor can deadlock the pool.
zip_futures_over resolves only when all futures resolve and value! re-raises the first rejection, so partial aggregates need explicit rescue/future chaining.
